definition: Motif means a distinctive element — an image, phrase, or design — that repeats throughout a work of art, literature, or music, gaining force with each return.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word motif. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know motif should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Interlocking waves ripple across the hotel's carpets, curtains, and tilework — a motif the designer carried into every room.
An echo is fainter than a motif: an image may echo once or twice across a work, while a motif returns so often that the repetition itself begins to carry meaning.
A leitmotif goes further than a motif: a motif recurs freely, but a leitmotif is bound by design to one character or idea and sounds every time that presence enters.

Theme means the idea a work keeps exploring, stated in the abstract — loyalty, decay, forgiveness. A theme is an idea; a motif is the concrete image, phrase, or figure that keeps returning to carry it.

Refrain means the repeated line of a song or poem, coming back word for word in its fixed place. A motif returns too, but freely — in new forms, new keys, new corners of the work — rather than as an exact repeat.

Symbol means an image or object that stands for a larger idea — and it can do that in a single appearance. A motif earns its force by returning again and again, whether or not it stands for anything at all.

Halfway through the songwriting workshop, Elena noticed that a three-note falling figure kept surfacing in her ballad — under the first verse, beneath the bridge, and again, slowed to half speed, in the final chorus.
She stopped fighting the motif and made it the song's signature.
One small musical figure, returning in verse, bridge, and chorus until the repetition itself stitches the song together — a recurring element like that is exactly what a motif is.

Motif belongs to the vocabulary of analysis: reviewers, art historians, and English teachers reach for it when a work repeats itself on purpose.
It applies as easily to wallpaper as to literature — a paisley motif, a betrayal motif.
Keep it apart from theme (the abstract idea) and from symbol (the stand-in): a motif need not mean anything at all; it need only return.
Watch the sound-alike motto, which is a saying to live by, not a repeating element.

Assembling the painter Iris Chen's fifty-year retrospective, curator Malik Rowe hung the canvases in order and noticed what reviewers had missed.
A red kite appears in her earliest student work, small and far away.
It returns in the harbor scenes of her middle years, tangled in rigging, and again in the late desert paintings, reduced to a diamond of color on the horizon.
Rowe stopped calling it a coincidence and began calling it a motif: the kite changes size, setting, and even shape, but it keeps coming back, and each return gathers up the ones before.
In the catalog he wrote that by the final room the kite no longer needs the sky — a red diamond on a kitchen table is enough to make visitors think of flight.
Chen, asked about it at the opening, only smiled and said that some images refuse to be finished with a painter.
